knowledge_type_note: A dynamic advantage — a positional concept whose defining property is that it EXPIRES. That distinguishes it from static concepts like a weak square, and it is why the same evaluation means different things depending on which kind of advantage produced it.

attributions.note: His enumeration of advantages splits them into permanent and temporary, which is where the initiative's defining property comes from. ACCESS CAVEAT: taken from a community study, not from Steinitz's text.

history.notes: Ordinary chess vocabulary; no coinage claimed. The classification of the initiative as a temporary advantage is conventionally Steinitz's, but the only source consulted for that here is a community study, so confidence is low. Worth verifying against The Modern Chess Instructor, which this project already has access to.

engine_era_note: Engines evaluate the initiative implicitly and are notably better than humans at telling a real initiative from a series of checks that achieve nothing. The concept is unrevised; what engines correct is the human tendency to overvalue forcing moves.

preconditions: One side is making threats the other must answer
The answering side has no time for a plan of their own
indicators_for: A sequence of forcing moves is available
The opponent's last several moves were all forced or defensive
A lead in development in an open position
The opponent's king is stuck in the centre
indicators_against: The threats can be answered by a move that also improves their position
The position is closed, so threats are hard to generate
The opponent can trade queens or simplify
The forcing moves have run out and nothing has been achieved
false_positive_traps: A series of checks is not an initiative. If the opponent's forced replies improve their position, you are helping them.
Having more active pieces is not the same as having the initiative — the test is whether they must answer you.
The initiative is invisible to a static feature scan, so it cannot be detected from the board alone; it is a property of the sequence.

typical_plans: Keep making threats so the opponent never gets a free move
Convert it into something permanent before it expires — material, structure, or a weak square
Sacrifice material to obtain or prolong it
As the defender: return material, trade queens, or find the move that both parries and improves
tactical_consequences: Forcing sequences that end in material or mate
strategic_consequences: Decays if not used — the defining property
The commonest form of compensation for a sacrifice

exceptions: It expires. An initiative that is not converted into something permanent is worth nothing afterwards.
A series of forcing moves is not an initiative if the replies help the opponent.
Black can hold it. It is not White's by right of the first move.
limitations: Recognition confidence LOW, and it is not detectable from a static position at all — it is a property of the sequence of moves, like the zwischenzug.
misconceptions: That the initiative is the same as being better. A worse position can hold the initiative, and often that is the only reason it survives.
That checks and captures create an initiative. They create forcing moves, which is not the same thing.
That it is White's by right.

conflicts.resolution: Opposed in tempo, not in truth. The two-weaknesses method requires TIME — fix, improve every piece, do not hurry — which is exactly what a player holding the initiative cannot afford to spend. Which applies depends on whether the advantage is dynamic or static: convert an initiative before it expires, accumulate a static edge slowly.

by_level.beginner: You are the one making threats, so your opponent has to keep answering instead of doing what they want.
by_level.intermediate: You have the initiative. It does not last — turn it into something permanent, like material or a lasting weakness, before it runs out.
by_level.advanced: A dynamic advantage: it decays. The question is what it can be converted into before the opponent consolidates.
by_level.master: Temporary by definition, and therefore in direct tension with slow methods like the two weaknesses. Price the conversion, not the initiative itself.

by_depth.short: You are making the threats; they are answering.
by_depth.normal: The initiative: your opponent has to answer your threats rather than pursue their own plans. It is temporary — one slow move lets them consolidate — so it has to be converted into something permanent while it lasts.
by_depth.deep: The state of setting the problems. Its defining property is that it expires, which puts it firmly on the dynamic side of Steinitz's split between permanent and temporary advantages and produces the standing instruction to use it or lose it. It is built out of tempi — a tempo is one move, the initiative is the sustained state — and it is the commonest compensation for a real sacrifice: when material is given for 'time', this is what is bought. The usual error is mistaking a run of forcing moves for an initiative; if the forced replies improve the opponent's position, the checks are helping them.

explanations.lesson: The initiative is a wasting asset. Ask what you are going to have left when the threats run out — and if the answer is nothing, you did not have an initiative.

avoid: the initiative means you are better

definition_short: The state of being the one making threats — the opponent must answer rather than pursue their own plans. It is temporary and must be used or lost.
definition_long:
Whoever is setting the problems has the initiative. The opponent's moves are answers rather than plans, and every tempo spent answering is one they cannot spend improving.

Its defining property is that it is TEMPORARY. Unlike a weak square or a damaged structure, it decays: one slow or decorative move lets the defender consolidate and it is gone. That is what puts it on the dynamic side of Steinitz's division of advantages into permanent and temporary, and it is why the standing instruction attached to it is 'use it or lose it'.

Relation to TEMPO: a tempo is one move; the initiative is the sustained state built from repeatedly gaining them. Relation to a LEAD IN DEVELOPMENT: development is the raw material, the initiative is what it can be converted into if converted quickly.

It is also the most common form of compensation for a sacrifice. When Spielmann's real sacrifice buys 'time', this is what is meant: a sequence of threats the opponent must answer, each one denying them a free move.

The first move gives White a small initial initiative, but it is not White's by right — Black takes it with counterplay, central breaks, or rapid development whenever they create the threats that must be answered.
